narrative_beats:
# Three Scene-Level Beats for *The HOA Board Will Now Come to Order*

---

## Beat 1: The Fine on the Ramp — Meredith receives the violation notice, buries her husband, and decides to go to war.

**Concrete Action:** Meredith Chen finds the HOA violation letter in the mailbox — $50 per day, compounding, for an "unauthorized structural modification" that is, in fact, the wheelchair ramp her dying husband needed to leave his own house. She appeals. Doug Whitmore denies the appeal personally, smiling warmly, expressing sympathy, bringing banana bread, and explaining that the bylaws are the bylaws. Her husband dies. The fines do not stop. The compounding does not stop. Meredith — a retired actuary, a woman who spent forty years quantifying risk — sits at her kitchen table with the HOA's governing documents and begins to read them not as a homeowner but as an adversary. She starts making calls. The disgraced court stenographer (a neighbor, removed from the courthouse for an outburst of conscience during a sentencing). The Robert's Rules enthusiast (a lonely man who has waited his entire life for parliamentary procedure to matter). Her book club, five women who have been reading about power for decades and are ready, at last, to exercise some. Meredith does not pitch revenge. She pitches *procedure*. She tells them: we are going to attend the annual meeting, and we are going to follow every rule, and we are going to take his organization apart from the inside using the very documents he hides behind. The team assembles not because they all loved Meredith's husband — some barely knew him — but because every single one of them has a fine, a denial, a humiliation, a fence-height letter folded and refolded in a kitchen drawer. The ramp is the catalyst. The reservoir was already full.

**Narrative Technique — The inciting wound as structural thesis statement, delivered through bureaucratic violence:** The story does not open with grief. It opens with a *letter*. Carver opened "Cathedral" with tone; this story opens with a document — the violation notice — because the entire narrative operates in the register of institutional language weaponized against human beings. The fine is not dramatic in the cinematic sense. It is dramatic in the actuarial sense: it is compounding. It is relentless. It is automatic. Doug does not need to be cruel in person because the system is cruel on his behalf, and this is the story's foundational insight — that tyranny in the suburban register does not look like tyranny; it looks like policy. The banana bread is not a comic detail. It is the story's most important image in this beat, because it is the mechanism by which Doug maintains his self-narrative as a good man. He is not denying a dying man a wheelchair ramp. He is upholding community standards. The bread is his proof. Meredith's transformation from grieving wife to strategic adversary must happen not through a dramatic monologue but through the specific act of *reading* — sitting with the bylaws and seeing them clearly for the first time, the way a chess player suddenly sees the board. This is an actuary's revenge: she will not argue with the system. She will *use* the system. The team assembly functions as an ensemble roll call, but the technique beneath it is **solidarity built from accumulated small wounds**. Each recruit carries their own violation letter. The story needs us to understand that Meredith is not recruiting soldiers — she is discovering that the army already exists, atomized by shame, waiting to be organized. The structural thesis is stated here in full: the same rules that oppress can liberate, if you read them more carefully than the oppressor does.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The compounding. The fine doesn't arrive once — it *compounds*, a word Meredith the actuary understands in her bones. Her husband is dead and the number keeps growing, accruing against a ramp that now leads to a door no wheelchair will ever pass through again. That detail — the ramp still there, the man gone, the fines still coming — is the story's emotional black hole, the thing that makes procedural comedy possible without ever becoming glib. We laugh at the bylaws later because we felt the ramp first. And Doug's banana bread — the dissonance between the warmth of the gesture and the coldness of the policy — establishes the story's central villain problem: Doug is not a monster. He is a man who has confused the maintenance of order with the practice of goodness, and the distance between those two things is where all the damage lives.

---

## Beat 2: The Preparation and the Fracture — The team masters the bylaws, discovers the embezzlement, rehearses the coup, and splits over whether they are the heroes or the next tyrants.

**Concrete Action:** Weeks of preparation. The stenographer transcribes every past meeting minute they can find, building a paper trail of Doug's procedural irregularities — votes taken without quorum, amendments never properly ratified, a decade of governance that is technically illegitimate. The Robert's Rules enthusiast conducts rehearsals in Meredith's living room, drilling the book club on points of order, motions to table, the specific language required to call for a vote of no confidence. They are earnest and they are ruthless and they are, at times, absurd — five women and two odd men practicing parliamentary combat over coffee cake. Then the book club treasurer, cross-referencing the HOA's published budgets against county landscaping invoices, finds it: the mulch fund. Fifteen years of discrepancies. Thousands of dollars. Not grand larceny — petty, sustained, almost pathological skimming. The PowerPoint is built. It is devastating. It is footnoted. Meanwhile, Doug senses something. He doesn't know what, but he has the animal instinct of every small-domain autocrat — he can feel the atmospheric change. He begins counter-maneuvering: calls an emergency session to amend the quorum threshold, attempts to move the annual meeting date, deploys selective bylaw interpretations through allies on the board. Each countermove is itself a minor procedural violation, and the stenographer logs every one. But then the fracture. It happens during a rehearsal. Someone — perhaps the Robert's Rules enthusiast, perhaps one of the book club members who has been reading too much about revolutions — says the thing that has been hovering over every meeting: *Are we any different?* They are using the bylaws as weapons. They are building a case designed not to reform Doug but to *destroy* him — publicly, completely, in front of his neighbors. The enthusiasm has curdled into something that feels less like justice and more like the thing they are fighting against, just wearing different clothes. Meredith's book club splits. Not cleanly — nothing in this story breaks cleanly — but enough that the coalition wobbles. Some want to offer Doug a chance to resign quietly. Others want the PowerPoint. Meredith, the actuary, the woman who measures everything, has to decide what this is actually for: her husband, or her anger, or something she cannot yet name.

**Narrative Technique — Procedural comedy as moral laboratory, with the ensemble as distributed conscience:** This beat is where the story earns its tonal complexity. The rehearsals are genuinely funny — the image of a book club drilling Roberts Rules motions has inherent comic energy — but Carver's lesson applies here in a different register: the comedy must be load-bearing. Every comedic rehearsal scene must simultaneously advance the procedural competence of the team *and* reveal the characters' deepening investment in a process that is changing them. The Robert's Rules enthusiast is the key figure here — a man who has lived in the abstract architecture of parliamentary procedure and is now, for the first time, watching it applied to real human stakes. His excitement is genuine, and it should unsettle us slightly, because we recognize the same pleasure Doug takes in enforcing bylaws, just redirected. This is the beat's central technique: **the mirror structure**. The story must place Meredith's team and Doug's governance in explicit parallel without editorializing about it. Doug believes the bylaws justify his power. Meredith believes the bylaws justify her resistance. They are both right, and the story's moral tension lives in the question of whether procedural correctness and moral correctness are the same thing. The embezzlement discovery functions as the team's moral permission slip — it transforms the coup from "angry homeowners versus petty bureaucrat" into "citizens exposing genuine corruption" — but the story must resist letting this discovery resolve the ethical tension too neatly. The mulch fund theft is real, but the desire to destroy Doug preceded its discovery. They were going to do this anyway. The embezzlement just makes it easier to feel righteous about it. The fracture scene is the structural hinge. It is the moment where the story refuses to be a simple revenge fantasy and becomes something more honest: an examination of what happens when justified anger meets the machinery of power and begins to enjoy the machinery more than the justice. Doug's counter-maneuvers in this beat must be rendered with the same procedural specificity as Meredith's preparations, because the story's final confrontation depends on both sides being *fluent* in the same language. The annual meeting must feel like a clash between two prepared adversaries, not an ambush.

**What Makes It Memorable:** The mulch fund. Not millions. Not a Ponzi scheme. *Mulch*. The smallness of the embezzlement is essential, because it perfectly mirrors the smallness of Doug's tyranny — the fence heights, the ramp fines, the compounding $50. This is a story about the enormous consequences of small-scale power, and the embezzlement must match that scale. Fifteen years of skimming the mulch budget while bringing banana bread to meetings is a portrait of self-deception so complete it becomes almost sympathetic, and that near-sympathy is what makes the fracture scene hit. When the team member asks *Are we any different?*, the question has teeth because the answer is genuinely unclear. Meredith sitting with that question — a woman who spent her career calculating probabilities, now facing an outcome she cannot quantify — is the emotional center of the entire story. The structural principle is borrowed directly from the Cathedral template: **delayed intimacy through elimination of alternatives.** By the end of this beat, every escape route has been closed. They cannot go back to simply being angry homeowners. They cannot unknow what they know about the mulch fund. They cannot pretend the coup is purely righteous. The only way out is through the meeting. The funnel narrows.

---

## Beat 3: The Annual Meeting — The procedural coup unfolds, Doug is exposed, and Meredith discovers what the fight was actually for.

**Concrete Action:** The meeting room. Folding chairs. A plastic table with a coffee urn. Doug at the front, smiling warmly, banana bread on a paper plate at his elbow. He calls the meeting to order. He does not know that Meredith's team has spent the last two weeks going door to door, collecting proxies, confirming attendance commitments, ensuring a quorum so unassailable that Doug's emergency threshold amendment — itself improperly ratified, as the stenographer can prove — is irrelevant. The room is full. Fuller than any annual meeting in memory. Doug notices. His smile holds. The procedural assault begins with a point of order from the Robert's Rules enthusiast, who rises with the calm, trembling joy of a man whose entire life has been building toward this moment: the previous meeting's minutes were never properly approved, which means every motion passed at that meeting is technically pending, which means the emergency bylaw amendments Doug rammed through are void. Doug objects. The stenographer reads back his own words from a meeting three years ago in which he argued the identical procedural point against a homeowner who wanted to challenge a fence ruling. His own precedent traps him. Motion by motion, amendment by amendment, the team dismantles his procedural architecture. Doug does not crumble — this is essential — he *fights*. He is genuinely intelligent within his domain. He parlays, he delays, he calls for recesses, he appeals to the room's desire for normalcy. Some of the assembled homeowners shift uncomfortably. This is taking too long. This feels too much like a trial. Then the PowerPoint. The mulch fund. Fifteen years of invoices, county records, budget discrepancies, presented in the actuary's clean, merciless columns. Doug's face. Not anger — *confusion*. He has told himself a story about this money for so long that the exposure reads to him not as justice but as betrayal. He says, quietly, that everything he did was for the neighborhood. He believes it. The vote of no confidence passes. Doug is removed. The room is silent in the way rooms are silent after something irreversible. And then Meredith is standing at the front of the room — the room wants her to take the presidency, the logical culmination, the hero's assumption of power — and she looks at the bylaws spread on the table, the same document she read at her kitchen table weeks ago, the document that killed her husband's dignity and that just saved hers. She does not take the chair. She proposes — in proper parliamentary form, seconded immediately by the Robert's Rules enthusiast, who is weeping — an amendment to the governing documents: a humanitarian variance clause. Any structural modification required for medical necessity is automatically approved. No vote required. No fine. No appeal. The amendment passes unanimously. Meredith sits down. The ramp is still standing outside her house. The meeting is adjourned.

**Narrative Technique — Procedural climax as emotional revelation, with the refusal of power as the transformative act:** The annual meeting scene must be the story's longest sustained set piece, and its success depends on a technique directly analogous to the cathedral-drawing scene in Carver: **the physical and procedural specifics must carry the emotional weight without the narrator or any character articulating the emotion explicitly.** The points of order, the motions, the quorum counts — these are not obstacles to the emotional climax; they *are* the emotional climax. The story has spent two beats teaching us to read parliamentary procedure as a language of human power, and now that language must be deployed with the fluency and intensity of any thriller's final confrontation. Doug's response to the PowerPoint is the beat's most critical character moment and the story's deepest structural echo of "Cathedral." Doug is the narrator of his own life, and in his narrative, he is the benevolent steward. The embezzlement is, in his accounting, justified — maintenance costs he covered, personal expenses that were really community investments, a story so practiced it has become his identity. When the numbers appear on the screen, we must feel — even for a moment — something other than triumph. We must feel the vertigo of a man watching his self-conception dissolve in a room full of his neighbors. This is **the villain's Cathedral moment**: the instant where the story insists on a character's full humanity at the exact moment we are most ready to dismiss it. Without this beat, the story is a revenge fantasy. With it, the story is about the human cost of institutional power on *every* person it touches, including the person wielding it. Meredith's refusal to take the presidency is the structural equivalent of the narrator closing his eyes. It is the moment where the expected trajectory — accumulate power, assume power, become the new authority — is rejected in favor of something the character could not have planned or anticipated. The amendment is not revenge. It is not even reform in the grand sense. It is one specific clause, aimed at one specific kind of suffering, and its smallness is its enormity. Meredith the actuary, who spent her life calculating large outcomes from small inputs, finally produces the calculation that matters: one ramp equals one life's dignity, and no governing document should have the power to deny it. The technique is **structural restraint at the moment of maximum narrative potential.** The story could end with Meredith in power. It ends instead with Meredith in her chair, the meeting adjourned, the ramp still standing. The funnel has reached its narrowest point, and what has passed through it is not a victory but a *change* — in the bylaws, and in the woman who changed them.

**What Makes It Memorable:** Doug's face when the PowerPoint appears. Not the villain's snarl. The confused, wounded bewilderment of a man who genuinely does not understand what he has done, because the story he has told himself is seamless and load-bearing and it has just been demolished in the room where he served coffee for fifteen years. That face is the story's moral achievement — it is the moment that separates this from satire and makes it fiction, because it insists that the antagonist is also a person who will drive home tonight and sit in a house that suddenly means something different, in a neighborhood that has just told him who he actually was. And then the amendment.
narrative_story:
# The HOA Board Will Now Come to Order

---

## I.

The letter was dated the fourteenth, a Tuesday, which Meredith Chen would later note was the same day she had driven Frank to his last oncology appointment, the one where Dr. Petrossian stopped talking about treatment timelines and began talking about comfort. She found the envelope in the mailbox between a circular from the grocery store and a sympathy card from someone at the old firm. The return address read Cedarview Estates Homeowners Association, and the typeface was the same officious serif the Association used for everything — meeting agendas, holiday reminders, notices about trash can placement on non-collection days.

**RE: Violation Notice — Unauthorized Structural Modification**
**Property: 4412 Briarwood Court**
**Nature of Violation: Installation of non-approved accessory structure (ramp, front entrance) without prior Architectural Review Committee submission, in contravention of Article IX, Section 3(b) of the Cedarview Estates CC&Rs.**
**Fine: $50.00 per day, compounding at 1.5% monthly on unpaid balance, effective retroactively to date of installation (October 2).**

She read it standing at the mailbox with her purse still on her shoulder. She read it again at the kitchen table. The ramp had been installed on October second because on October first Frank had come home from the hospital in a wheelchair, and the two concrete steps leading to the front door of the house they had lived in for twenty-three years had become, overnight, a wall.

The contractor had come the next morning. He was a young man named Tomás who had built ramps for the VA hospital and who measured the slope with a level and said he could have it done by afternoon. He did. It was pressure-treated pine with a non-slip surface and a handrail on both sides and it met every specification of the Americans with Disabilities Act, a fact that would prove irrelevant, because the ADA did not apply to private homeowner associations, as the letter's second page explained in a paragraph that had clearly been drafted by someone who enjoyed explaining this.

Meredith appealed. The process required a written submission to the Architectural Review Committee, which was Doug Whitmore and two people Doug Whitmore had appointed, and a fourteen-day waiting period, during which the fine continued to accrue. She submitted the appeal with a letter from Dr. Petrossian, a photograph of the ramp, and a copy of the ADA specifications, which she included not because it was legally relevant but because she wanted them to see it.

Doug came to the house on a Saturday. He brought banana bread. It was wrapped in plastic wrap with a small bow, and he carried it cupped in both hands like an offering, and he stood on the ramp he was fining her for and rang the doorbell and smiled when she opened the door.

"Meredith," he said. "May I come in?"

He sat at the kitchen table. He asked about Frank. He listened with his head tilted and his hands folded and he said, "I am so sorry you're going through this." He said it the way people say it when they mean it and also when they're about to say *but*.

"The committee reviewed your appeal," he said. He broke off a corner of banana bread for himself, a gesture of informality, of neighborliness, of *we're-all-in-this-together*. "And I wish I could tell you differently. I do. But the bylaws are the bylaws, Meredith. If we make an exception for one modification, we open the door for everyone, and then what do we have? You understand. You're a numbers person."

She was. She had been an actuary for Midwestern Mutual for thirty-eight years. She had spent her professional life calculating the statistical probability of catastrophe — the likelihood of flood, of fire, of a healthy thirty-four-year-old developing a terminal illness, of a house built on stable ground shifting on its foundation. She understood risk. She understood compounding.

"The fine is compounding," she said.

"I know. And I want you to know that's not my choice. That's in the documents. Section twelve, paragraph eight. The compounding schedule is automatic. It's in there to incentivize timely compliance, not to punish anyone."

"Frank can't get into the house without the ramp."

"I understand that. And I want to be clear — nobody is asking you to remove the ramp right now. We're just asking you to submit a proper ARC application so we can work toward a resolution that's consistent with community standards. The fine pauses as soon as the application is approved."

"You just denied the application."

"We denied the *appeal.* The application process is separate. There's a form. I can email it to you."

He emailed the form. It was eleven pages. It required a site plan, a materials specification, a neighbor impact assessment, and a $200 processing fee. It required the signature of the property owner, which was Frank, who could no longer hold a pen without his hand shaking so badly the signature would be illegible, and who died on November ninth, a Thursday, at 4:15 in the afternoon, in the hospital bed that Meredith had rented and set up in the living room so he could see the dogwood tree through the front window.

The funeral was on a Monday. Forty people came. Doug was one of them. He wore a dark suit and he shook Meredith's hand and he said, "Frank was a good man and a good neighbor." He brought banana bread.

On Tuesday the mail came. In it was a notice from the Cedarview Estates Homeowners Association informing her that her outstanding balance for the ongoing violation at 4412 Briarwood Court was $2,137.50, reflecting forty-one days of non-compliance at $50 per day plus accrued compounding interest, and that failure to resolve the violation within thirty days would result in the placement of a lien on the property.

Meredith sat at the kitchen table. The banana bread from the funeral was still on the counter, untouched, the plastic wrap still on. Outside, through the window Frank had looked through in his last weeks, the ramp descended from the front door to the walkway. It was well built. The handrail was smooth and the slope was gentle and it led to a door that no wheelchair would ever pass through again, and the fine on it was growing by $50 a day plus 1.5% monthly and it would keep growing, she understood, until she removed it or paid it or the numbers became large enough to take her house. The math was not complicated. She was an actuary. She knew how compounding worked. It was the most patient force in the universe.

She took the CC&Rs from the drawer where she kept household documents — the mortgage, the deed, the insurance policy, the HOA file. She had read them once, twenty-three years ago, the way you read terms and conditions: scanning, trusting, assuming the document existed to protect you. Now she opened to page one and began to read the way she had once read actuarial tables — not for the general sense but for every specific, every exception, every clause and sub-clause and defined term, every place where the language was precise and every place where it was not.

She read for three hours. She made notes in the margins in pencil, small and neat, the handwriting of a woman who had spent a career writing in margins. When she finished, she went back to the beginning and read again. By the end of the second reading she had filled four pages of a yellow legal pad with references, cross-references, and questions. By the end of the third reading the questions had become observations and the observations had begun to harden into something structural — a pattern, a series of gaps between what the bylaws required and what Doug Whitmore actually did, a distance between the document and its implementation that was not a flaw in the system but was, in fact, the system itself.

She picked up the phone.

---

Bonnie Okafor lived on the next block over, in a house with a fence that was four inches too tall. The HOA had fined her $600 for the fence. The fence had been built to that height because Bonnie's ex-husband had spent the six months after the divorce sitting in his car across the street at varying hours, and four inches was the difference between being able to see him and not being able to see him, and the Architectural Review Committee had denied her variance request because the CC&Rs specified forty-two inches and her fence was forty-six and, as Doug had explained, the bylaws were the bylaws.

Before the fence, before the divorce, before any of it, Bonnie had been a court stenographer in the County Superior Court for nineteen years. She had been removed — officially, she had resigned; functionally, she had been removed — after an incident during the sentencing phase of a DUI case in which the defendant, a twenty-year-old kid, was sentenced to six years and Bonnie had stopped typing, looked up at the judge, and said, clearly enough for it to be entered into the record by the substitute stenographer who replaced her: "He's somebody's son and you know this is wrong and you're doing it anyway." She had not been wrong. The conviction was later overturned on appeal. This did not get her job back.

What Bonnie had, besides an illegally tall fence and a stenographer's memory for the exact words people used, was a Steno machine in her living room that she kept oiled and functional the way a retired surgeon might keep a scalpel sharp — not to use, but to remain a person who could use it.

"I need transcripts," Meredith said. "Of every HOA meeting. And I need them verbatim."

Bonnie was quiet for a moment. Then she said: "I have three years' worth of recordings on my phone. I started recording when he denied my fence appeal. I just sit in the back and let it run."

"How are the recordings?"

"The audio's clean. He projects."

"Of course he does."

"Meredith, what are you doing?"

Meredith told her. Bonnie was quiet for a longer moment. Then she said, "What time do you want me there?"

---

Gerald Fitzroy lived alone in a townhouse at the end of the development, Unit 14-C, and had lived there for eleven years, during which time he had attended every single HOA meeting, including four emergency sessions, two budget ratification hearings, and the special election of 2019, which was conducted by show of hands despite the fact that Article IV, Section 7(a) clearly required a paper ballot for any election in which more than one candidate was nominated, a procedural violation Gerald had raised at the time and that had been dismissed by Doug as "not meaningful to the outcome," a phrase Gerald could still quote from memory because it was, in his view, the single most dangerous sentence in the English language.

Gerald had discovered Robert's Rules of Order in 1987, during a period of his life he did not discuss in detail but which involved a great deal of solitude and a library card. He had read the book the way some people read scripture — for structure, for meaning, for the reassurance that somewhere, someone had sat down and determined the correct way for human beings to make decisions together, and that the correct way was knowable, and consistent, and fair, provided everybody followed it. He had the current edition and two prior editions and a spiral-bound notebook in which he had, over many years, catalogued every parliamentary situation he had ever encountered and cross-referenced it to the relevant section of Robert's Rules, sometimes with annotations on where the Rules were, in his opinion, insufficient — which was rarely, but occasionally, in matters of subsidiary motions.

Nobody had ever asked Gerald to use this knowledge for anything that mattered.

Meredith asked.

She called him on a Wednesday evening, introduced herself — they had spoken perhaps twice, both times at meetings — and told him what she needed: someone who knew Robert's Rules well enough to deploy them under pressure, in real time, against an adversary who used them selectively and badly.

Gerald was quiet for so long that Meredith checked if the call had dropped.

"Mrs. Chen," he said. "I have been waiting for a very long time for someone to take this seriously."

"I'm taking it seriously."

"He chaired the 2021 budget meeting without establishing a quorum. I counted the room. There were fourteen people present. The quorum threshold is twenty. I raised the issue. He said presence was implied by proxy. That is not a thing. That is not a thing in Robert's Rules, it is not a thing in the CC&Rs, it is not a thing in any parliamentary authority recognized on this planet. I have a letter. I wrote a letter. I sent the letter. The letter was not acknowledged."

"Gerald."

"I have the letter. I have a copy."

"Bring the letter. Bring everything. Can you come Thursday at seven?"

"I can come Thursday at six."

---

The book club met every other Tuesday in rotating houses and had, for the past three years, been reading with a thematic focus that one of its members described as "systems of power" and another described as "the bastards" and a third described as "honestly, it started with *The Handmaid's Tale* and just kept going." They had read Atwood, Solzhenitsyn, Arendt, a biography of Robert Moses, two histories of redlining, and, most recently, a slim book about the topology of fascism that one of them had found in a university bookshop and that they had discussed for four meetings because it argued, convincingly, that authoritarianism did not require charisma or ideology — only procedural capture of small institutions by patient individuals who understood that most people do not read the rules, and that this is enough.

The members were: Helen Park, sixty-seven, retired school administrator, whose garden shed had been fined because it was painted a shade of green not on the approved palette, the approved palette containing eleven shades of green, none of which matched the shade Helen had used, which was, according to Doug, "clearly teal." Jean Mackey, seventy-one, whose outdoor holiday lights had incurred a violation for remaining up until January 22, three days past the January 19 deadline, because Jean's son was supposed to take them down and Jean's son had the flu and Jean could not reach the gutters and Doug had expressed sympathy and also issued the fine. Patricia Huang, sixty-six, whose formal complaint about the dead ash tree on the HOA common ground behind her property — a tree that was shedding limbs onto her patio, one of which had cracked the glass on her outdoor table — had been "received" seventeen months ago and neither resolved nor acknowledged since. Denise Carter, sixty-nine, whose request to install a doorbell camera had been denied on the grounds that exterior-mounted electronics required ARC approval, which Denise had then applied for, and which had been denied on the grounds that the camera's sightline included a portion of the common walkway, which constituted a "surveillance encroachment" — a term that appeared nowhere in the CC&Rs. And Ruth Abernathy, seventy-three, who had no personal violation but who had been friends with Meredith for forty years and who, when Meredith called and said, "I need the club," said only: "It's time, isn't it?"

Meredith did not pitch revenge. She sat in her living room on a Thursday evening with Bonnie and Gerald and the five women of the book club and she laid the CC&Rs on the coffee table and she said:

"The annual meeting is in six weeks. Article IV, Section 2, requires that the meeting be held on the date specified in the governing documents. He cannot move it without a two-thirds vote of the membership, which he has not obtained. Article IV, Section 5, specifies the quorum threshold: twenty percent of eligible voting members, in person or by valid proxy. There are two hundred and twelve homes in Cedarview Estates. Quorum is forty-three. He has not had a legitimate quorum in at least three years. Every motion he has passed in that time is voidable."

She paused. Gerald was nodding so vigorously that his glasses were migrating down his nose.

"I am not proposing that we argue with him," Meredith said. "I am not proposing that we yell, or complain, or make speeches. I am proposing that we attend the annual meeting with a valid quorum of our own, that we follow every rule in this document more precisely than he has ever followed any of them, and that we use the procedures he has been ignoring for fifteen years to remove him from the board."

Helen Park picked up the CC&Rs and opened to a page she had evidently already been reading. "The motion for a vote of no confidence," she said. "Article IV, Section 9(c). Requires a simple majority of members present and voting."

"Yes."

"He's never had a room bigger than twenty people. If we pack the room—"

"We don't pack anything. We establish a quorum. We follow the agenda. And when we reach new business, we follow Section 9(c)."

"And if he calls
